Most of us are first exposed to spies and secret agents through movies and books. Films like James Bond and Mission Impossible thrill and entertain us. The cool main characters stay calm and collected in the most intense situations. Scenes with wiretapping, laser-trapped rooms, and disguises enthrall us. Hollywood spies live life on the edge and almost always get the bad guys in the end. Spies and secret agents have captivated novelists and filmmakers for hundreds of years. They don’t just exist on screen and in books, though. They have been around since ancient times and live among us today. While the United States Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) does not use the word “spy,” they have undercover agents or field operatives to carry out missions. They get information, investigate enemy or criminal behavior, and conduct covert operations. CIA agents report to the Director of National Intelligence appointed by the President.

Espionage is the act of gathering information through spies, secret agents, or monitoring devices. These actions are often carried out for political or military purposes. The Art of War, written by Chinese theorist Sun Tzu in the 5th century BCE, discusses spying. He focused on preparing for enemy attacks rather than hoping they never come. He advised, "One who knows the enemy and knows himself will not be endangered in a hundred engagements." This text is still a reference for military and political action. Ancient civilizations, including the Greeks, Romans, Aztecs, Hebrews, and Mongols, had complex systems for gathering intelligence. Feudal Japan used “shinobi,” or ninjas, and the Aztecs used “pochtecas” to carry out covert missions. Ancient spies used many of the same methods as modern spies. They accessed key locations like castles, palaces, and temples. They dressed in disguises and spoke the languages of their enemies. Spies were most often used before battles and wars.

Accounts of espionage appear in some of the world’s earliest historical records. Egyptian pharaohs used spies to identify disloyal subjects and locate tribes to conquer. From 1000 BCE onward, Egyptian spies focused on their Greek and Roman rivals. Spies used secret language, codes, and trick inks to communicate. Egyptian spies were first to develop the extensive use of poisons to carry out assassinations or sabotage. The rise of the Greek empire brought new forms of law enforcement and military tactics. Greek armies used deception and surprise to attack their enemies, as seen in the legend of the Trojan Horse. The large wooden horse was brought to Troy as a gift, but it was a trick. Once the horse entered the heavily guarded city and night fell, hundreds of Greek soldiers crept out from the horse, killed the guards, and opened the doors of the city for the rest of their army.

The Romans created the largest empire in the ancient world. Their growth necessitated new political and military tactics. Rome relied heavily on intelligence information. They advanced spy tactics more than any other civilization in the ancient world. One of Rome’s most famous acts of espionage was the assassination of Julius Caesar in 44 BCE. Forty senators conspired against him and stabbed him to death in a meeting hall. The Romans used intelligence forces to spy on neighbors, convince tribal leaders to join the empire, and gauge the military strength of rivals. Spies disguised themselves in public spaces like markets to eavesdrop on people and gauge the political climate. Later, the Crusades and the Inquisition cemented the power of the Catholic Church in Europe. Like the Romans, the Church used spies to monitor the public and root out enemies. The Church denounced “heretics” or anyone who did not subscribe to their rules.
